Avoiding bonking in theory is simple – eat enough carbohydrates to convert into glucose to fill your glycogen stores. 

The problem is that you can only process 60g to 90g of carbohydrates an hour as discussed in what to eat on a long bike ride . 

So no matter how much you eat you can only convert so much of it to usable energy. 

Eating too much is a whole other can of worms… 

So if you are eating the correct amount then it will come down to monitoring intensity and making sure you are not exceeding your limit and staying properly hydrated.

Domenico Pozzovivo (born 30 November 1982) is an Italian professional road racing cyclist for UCI ProTeam AG2R La Mondiale. 

His very small stature confer him with the qualities of a pure climbing specialist. 

He is most known for a victory in stage 8 of the 2012 Giro d'Italia, an overall victory in the 2012 Giro del Trentino, and is notable for his high education.

Pozzovivo has a degree in economics and wrote a thesis entitled "Southern politics from the unity of Italy up to now". 

His high education has earned him the nickname "Dr. Pozzovivo" in the peloton. 

He stated that his fields of interest outside cycling are history, technology, economics, politics and weather forecasting.

He also speaks French fluently and stated that a jump into politics would interest him after his cycling career.

MORE THAN JUST AN ELITE PROFESSIONAL CYCLIST

If you’re following the British Cycling Training Plans, you’ll notice that rest days and easier recovery weeks are regularly scheduled in. These cycles of training and recovery are what stimulate gains in fitness but many riders who don’t follow structured training plans, simply believe more is more and end up plateauing, losing form or even becoming ill.

Ultimately, the objective of training is to improve performance. To do so we must place a training load on the body and mind to promote training adaptations. This training load is dependent on how hard, how long and how often we train (intensity/duration/frequency). We must also consider other factors such as work, travelling and day-to-day living as this also stresses the body. 

Read more at https://www.britishcycling.org.uk/knowledge/article/izn20140915-Training-Overtraining-and-Overreaching-0#9Ke5XQI3hkfksBYD.99

"Remember it’s quality of training not quantity that’ll get you results."

"Maintaining consistency in the core sessions and staying healthy and injury free are the keys to success."

Read more at https://www.britishcycling.org.uk/knowledge/article/izn20150120-Weeks-17-20---2014-15-Intermediate-training-plan-0#lZg84Z9bjF2gC5A2.99

Remember quality is far more important than quantity and if you’re unable to complete the workouts at the specified intensities, you won’t be gaining maximum benefit from them.
Read more at https://www.britishcycling.org.uk/knowledge/article/izn20150127-Weeks-17-20---2014-15-Advanced-training-plan-0#yQOmUV7QoXsmD0Lu.99

There is a trick to this.

Let us say you are riding far out away from anywhere you can find tires, but you have a pump.

Deflate your tube and pull the portion of the tube out from the tire so that you can wrap that portion of the tube.

We wrap that portion of the tube to make it stronger, because the tube is so flexible under pressure, it will burst out, and make the damage bigger.

Your tire will not last so long under these conditions.

Look around for old discarded packaging materials, such as the metalized foil plastic polymere bags in which laundry detergent is sold.

Use a kniife or scissors to cut a long patch that will wrap aound the tube in a single piece as much as possible.

A big patch, like 10 cm x 30 cm is great, if you can find a metalized polymere bag that big, which is possible if you carry such a spare bag or patch in your gear as you travel.

Don't wrap your patch around the tube too tight, or not too loose either.

Judge for yourself how tight is just about right for the situation.

Stuff your tube nicely back into the tire and pump up the tube firm, not too soft and not too hard given the condition of the tear.

If you have superglue on hand, that may help, but I never tried it.

Be gentle as you ride not hiting any rocks or bumps.

If you need to ride off road, better to walk your bike while you can still ride it on the road.

I was really impressed with the bike tower. Sent as much detail as I could for further research.

The bike tower can accommodate 116 bicycles.

To building itself cost around 300k USD (6mil CZK)

There can be found similar bike tower in Taiwan. 

This tower was the first one in the EU in 2013.

The parking take 35s.

The bike tower offers 380V power sockets for electric bikes.

Public air pump can be found there too.



Parking fee 0.25USD (5CZK) per day.

This tower is partly sponsored by a EU fund and the city's public finance.

Within 2.5 year, 35k biker been using it.

35k × 0.25 = 8,750 USD revenue from parking fee

With such low fees, clearly it is a public service .
Very low cost for user, but big initial investment.
